title: Line Plots with Fractions
description: Learn to read and create line plots with fractions for Class 4 Maths. Find totals, differences, and most common values from data. Includes ribbon length examples, 10 MCQs and 6 IMO questions.

topics.title: Understanding and Reading Line Plots
topics.concept:
A line plot (also called a dot plot) is a graph that shows data along a number line. Each X above the number line represents one piece of data.

Key terms:

  • Mode = most common value (where the most X's are)
  • Range = largest value minus smallest value
  • Total = each value multiplied by its count, then all added together

Line plots work with whole numbers AND fractions on the number line.

examples.problem: From the line plot above (ribbon lengths), how many ribbons are shown in total?
examples.solution: Count all X's: 2 (at 3 in) + 3 (at 3.5 in) + 2 (at 4 in) + 1 (at 4.5 in) = 8 ribbons.

examples.problem: What is the most common ribbon length?
examples.solution: The most X's are above 3.5 inches (3 ribbons). The most common length is 3.5 inches.

examples.problem: How many ribbons are longer than 3.5 inches?
examples.solution: At 4 inches: 2 ribbons. At 4.5 inches: 1 ribbon. Total = 3 ribbons longer than 3.5 inches.

recap: A line plot shows data using X marks above a number line
Each X represents ONE piece of data
The value with the most X's is the MODE (most common value)
Always count all X's carefully to find the total

topics.title: Creating Line Plots from Data
topics.concept:
How to Create a Line Plot:

  • Step 1: Find the range — identify the smallest and largest values
  • Step 2: Draw a number line with equal intervals covering all values
  • Step 3: Label the number line (use fractions where needed)
  • Step 4: Place one X above the number for each data point
  • Step 5: Give the plot a clear title

Line plots with fractions often use intervals of 1/4 or 1/2.

examples.problem: Create a line plot for ribbon lengths (cm): 5, 5.5, 5, 5.5, 6, 5.5, 5, 6
examples.solution: Range: 5 to 6. Draw number line from 5 to 6 with 0.5 intervals. At 5: 3 X's. At 5.5: 3 X's. At 6: 2 X's. Title: Ribbon Lengths (cm).

examples.problem: Data: apple weights (g): 140, 150, 150, 160, 150, 170, 160, 140. Create line plot and find the most common weight.
examples.solution: At 140g: 2 X's. At 150g: 3 X's. At 160g: 2 X's. At 170g: 1 X. Most common weight = 150g (most X's).

recap: First find the range (min and max values) before drawing
Use equal intervals on the number line — fractions must be equally spaced
Place one X for each data point — do not skip or double-count
Always give the line plot a descriptive title and label the units

topics.title: Finding Totals and Differences from Line Plots
topics.concept:
Line plots help us calculate quickly:

Finding Total: For each value, multiply it by the number of X's above it. Then add all products.

Finding Difference: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value shown on the plot.

Finding Average (Mean): Divide total by the number of data points (number of X's).

These skills apply to line plots with fractions too — multiply fractions by counts carefully!

examples.problem: A line plot shows stick lengths (ft): 2 sticks at 1 ft, 3 sticks at 2 ft, 1 stick at 3 ft. Find total length.
From the same plot, what is the difference between the longest and shortest stick?
examples.solution: Longest = 3 ft. Shortest = 1 ft. Difference = 3 - 1 = 2 feet.

examples.problem: Milk in glasses (cups): 1 glass at 1/2 cup, 3 glasses at 3/4 cup, 2 glasses at 1 cup. Total milk?

recap: Total = sum of (each value x number of X's at that value)
Difference = largest value minus smallest value on the plot
Mean = Total / number of data points
With fractions: multiply fraction by count carefully, then add all products

questions.q: Plants heights (cm) plot: 1 at 10, 2 at 15, 3 at 20, 2 at 25. Total height of all plants?
From the plants plot, 3 tallest plants are removed. New total height?
questions.explanation: Remove 2 at 25cm (50) and 1 at 20cm (20): 70 removed. Remaining: 150-70=80 cm.

questions.q: How many plants need to grow 5 cm more to reach exactly 25 cm?
questions.explanation: Plants at 20 cm (3 plants each need 5 cm more to reach 25 cm).

questions.q: Jumps plot: 2 at 2m, 2 at 2.5m, 2 at 3m, 2 at 3.5m (8 jumps). Average jump distance?

questions.explanation: Jumps at 3m or above: 2 at 3m + 2 at 3.5m = 4 jumps.

questions.q: Weights of parcels: 3 at 1/4 kg, 2 at 1/2 kg, 1 at 3/4 kg. A van carries max 2 kg. Can it carry all?
questions.explanation: (1/4x3)+(1/2x2)+(3/4x1)=3/4+1+3/4=2.5. Hmm 3/4+4/4+3/4=10/4=2.5 kg. Actually too much. So No. But option A says exactly 2: (3/4+2/2+3/4)? 3/4+1+3/4=1+6/4=1+1.5=2.5 kg. Answer: No. Correcting: answer is B.
